01.note: Rava was sitting with Rav Nahman as Rav Nahman was slipping into death. Rav Nahman asked Rava to tell the Angel of Death not to torment him. Rava answered that surely Rav Nahman was an important man in Heaven's eyes, but Rav Nahman replied that in the world above no one counts as important, honorable or complete. Rava asked him to appear in a dream after his death, and he did: dying, he said, was as painless as pulling a hair out of milk, yet if God told him to go back to life as before he would refuse, because the fear of the Angel of Death is so great.
01.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous died. This one comes right after the near-identical exchange between Rava and his brother Rav Seorim, and pairs with it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who sits with Rav Nahman at his death and later asks him in a dream what dying was like.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage on his deathbed who asks Rava to plead with the Angel of Death for him.

people.name: the Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, whom Rav Nahman imagines offering to send him back to life.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

02.note: The Angel of Death appeared to Rabbi Elazar while he was eating teruma. Rabbi Elazar objected that teruma is called sacred, so it would be wrong to die in the middle of eating it. The moment passed and he was spared.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous faced death. This is the first of a run of stories in which a Sage talks back to the Angel of Death.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who argues the Angel of Death out of taking him while he eats teruma.

terms.meaning: The portion of the harvest given to the priests. It is holy food, eaten only by priests and their households in a state of ritual purity.
In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

03.note: The Angel of Death appeared to Rav Sheshet in the marketplace. Rav Sheshet protested: should he die in the street like an animal? He told the Angel of Death to come to his house instead.
03.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous faced death. This follows the story of Rabbi Elazar, another Sage who tells the Angel of Death when and where he may take him.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who refuses to die in the marketplace and sends the Angel of Death to his home.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

04.note: The Angel of Death appeared to Rav Ashi in the marketplace. Rav Ashi asked for thirty days to review his learning, since in Heaven they say that happy is the one who arrives with his learning in hand. On the thirtieth day the Angel of Death came back. When Rav Ashi asked why he was in such a hurry, the angel answered that Rav Huna bar Natan, his successor, was already pressing at his heels, and one reign may not overlap another by even a hair's breadth.
04.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous faced death; this follows the stories of Rabbi Elazar and Rav Sheshet, who also bargain with the Angel of Death.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who wins thirty days from the Angel of Death to review his studies.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Natan
people.about: Named by the Angel of Death as the man ready to succeed Rav Ashi as leader.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

05.note: The Angel of Death could not take Rav Hisda, because his mouth never stopped reciting his studies. So the angel went and sat on the cedar beam of the study hall. The cedar cracked, Rav Hisda fell silent for a moment, and in that moment the angel was able to take him.
05.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous died; this follows a run of Sages who hold off the Angel of Death, here by unbroken Torah study.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage whose constant study keeps the Angel of Death away from him.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

06.note: The Angel of Death could not get near Rabbi Hiyya. One day he disguised himself as a poor man, knocked at the door and asked for bread, and Rabbi Hiyya brought it out to him. Then the angel said: you have mercy on a poor man, so why have you no mercy on me? He revealed who he was and showed Rabbi Hiyya a rod of fire, and Rabbi Hiyya gave himself up to him.
06.why: This is the last in the Gemara's series about how the righteous died, many of them resisting the Angel of Death; after it the Gemara turns to the next mishna, on mourning during the Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage the Angel of Death cannot approach until he tricks him with a request for charity.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

07.note: When Rabbi Yishmael's sons died, four elders came to comfort him: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Tarfon warned the others not to interrupt one another, and Rabbi Akiva asked to speak last. Rabbi Yishmael opened by blaming his own many sins for his repeated losses. Each elder then quoted a verse about a biblical figure who did only one good deed yet was mourned or honored at death (the sons of Aaron, Abijah son of Jeroboam, King Zedekiah, King Ahab) and argued that the sons of Rabbi Yishmael deserve all the more. Along the way the Gemara pauses to ask what Abijah's good deed was, and Rav Yosef says he would not understand Rabbi Akiva's verse without its Aramaic translation.
07.why: The Gemara has been gathering teachings on mourning and eulogies, such as Rabbi Meir's saying that whoever eulogizes others will be eulogized; this baraita shows Sages comforting a mourner. Afterward Rava questions how the verses about Zedekiah and Josiah fit together.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A great Sage, learned in aggada, whose sons have died.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: One of the four elders who comes to comfort Rabbi Yishmael; he sets the rule that no one interrupt.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: One of the four comforters; he speaks of Abijah son of Jeroboam.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: One of the four comforters; he speaks of King Zedekiah.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: One of the four comforters, who asks to speak last; he speaks of the mourning in Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara.
An argument from the lesser to the greater: if something is true in a weaker case, it is all the more true in a stronger one.
The non-legal teachings of the Sages: stories, sayings and interpretations of Scripture.
The Targum, an ancient Aramaic rendering of the Bible, which here explains an obscure verse.

08.note: Two mute men, grandsons (or, some say, nephews) of Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda, lived in the neighborhood of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. Whenever he entered the study hall they came in too, sat before the Sages, nodded their heads and moved their lips. Rabbi prayed for them and they were healed, and it turned out they had learned the Mishna, the Sifra, the Sifrei and the entire Talmud.
08.why: A baraita had said a mute person is exempt from the Temple assembly because he cannot learn. The Gemara brings this case to challenge that: these mute men did learn. Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi then reread the verse as 'that they may teach'.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the two mute men follow him into the study hall, and he prays for their healing.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda
people.about: The grandfather, or by another account the uncle, of the two mute men.

terms.meaning: An early collection of the Sages' legal interpretations of the book of Leviticus.
An early collection of the Sages' legal interpretations of Numbers and Deuteronomy.
Jewish law; here it means the Mishna, the core collection of legal teachings.

09.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma went to pay their respects to their teacher Rabbi Yehoshua in Peki'in. He asked what new idea had been taught in the study hall that day. They demurred, saying they were his students and all their learning came from him, but he insisted that a study hall is never without something new. They told him Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had lectured on the assembly verse 'the men, the women and the little ones': men come to learn, women to hear, and the little ones so that those who bring them are rewarded. Rabbi Yehoshua said they had held a fine pearl and tried to keep it from him. They began to report a second teaching of Rabbi Elazar's; the rest of the conversation comes after this excerpt.
09.why: The Gemara has been discussing who is obliged in the Temple assembly, deriving the exemption of deaf and mute people from that same verse. This baraita brings a homiletic reading of the verse.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: One of two students who visit Rabbi Yehoshua and report the day's lecture.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma
people.about: The other student who visits Rabbi Yehoshua with Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Their teacher, living in Peki'in, who presses them for the new idea taught that day.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: The Sage whose week it was to lecture in the study hall.

terms.meaning: Hakhel: the gathering of the whole people at the Temple on Sukkot after the Sabbatical Year, to hear the Torah read aloud (Deuteronomy 31).
To draw a teaching from a verse by close, creative reading of its words, beyond their plain sense.

09.flag: The story stops mid-conversation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's second teaching (in AFTER) and Rabbi Yehoshua's closing praise of him (on 3b) belong to the same story but fall outside the STORY segments.

10.note: Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskit went to greet Rabbi Eliezer in Lod, and Rabbi Eliezer asked what new idea had come up in the study hall that day. Rabbi Yosei told him the Sages had taken a vote and decided that in Ammon and Moab the poor man's tithe is separated in the Sabbatical Year. Rabbi Eliezer said to him in anger: Yosei, put out your hands and catch your eyes, and he did. Then Rabbi Eliezer wept, quoted 'The counsel of the Lord is with those who fear Him', and sent word that the Sages need not worry about their vote: he had a tradition from Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, reaching back to Moses at Sinai, that ruled the same way, and he explained the reason. Once he calmed down, he prayed that Rabbi Yosei's eyes return to their place, and they did.
10.why: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehoshua's students hesitated to tell him Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's new teachings. Its answer is this incident, in which a student who reported a new ruling to his teacher was struck blind.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskit
people.about: A student who visits Rabbi Eliezer and reports the Sages' vote.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage living in Lod; the translation also calls him Rabbi Elazar. He strikes Rabbi Yosei's eyes, then restores them.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's teacher, from whom he received the tradition about Ammon and Moab.

terms.meaning: A tenth of the produce given to the poor in certain years of the seven-year cycle.
Every seventh year, when the Land of Israel is left unworked and its produce is ownerless.

terms.term: halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai
terms.meaning: A law the Sages hold was given orally to Moses, with no verse behind it, and handed down teacher to student.
The holy status of the Land of Israel, which brings its special farming laws. The text says the first one, from the conquest after Egypt, held only for its own time.

11.note: The Angel of Death used to keep company with Rav Beivai bar Abaye. Once he told his agent to bring him Miriam who braided women's hair, and the agent brought Miriam who raised small children instead. Told of the mistake, the agent offered to return her, but the angel said that since she was here she should be counted among the dead. Rav Beivai asked how the agent could take her before her time; he said she had been lighting and sweeping the oven, set the shovel on her foot and was burned, her luck faltered, so he took her. Asked whether they had the right to do this, the angel quoted 'there are those swept away without justice', explained that he keeps such souls until their generation's years are complete, and said the lost years go to a Torah scholar who lets insults pass.
11.why: Rav Yosef wept at the verse 'there are those swept away without justice', asking whether anyone really dies before his time. The Gemara answers yes and brings this story to show it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who weeps at a verse suggesting people can die without justice.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: A Sage who kept company with the Angel of Death and questions him about a wrongful death.

people.name: Miriam
people.about: Two women of this name: one who braided women's hair, and one who raised babies and was taken by mistake.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time. Here he has agents who do the work for him.
The name of the angel the text says watches over the souls of the dead.

12.note: The Sages said to Rava that he seemed to escape both curses of the verse: God never hid His face from him, and the authorities took nothing from him. Rava replied that they did not know how many gifts he sent in secret to the house of King Shapur. Even so, the Sages cast their eyes on him. Meanwhile King Shapur's household sent for Rava and imprisoned him. Rava said this bore out the teaching of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that wherever the Sages cast their eyes, the result is either death or poverty.
12.why: Rav had just taught that anyone who never suffers God hiding His face, or being devoured by others, is not one of the Jewish people. The Sages raise this teaching against Rava, who seemed to be spared both.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose prayers were answered and who seemed safe from the authorities; he is imprisoned by King Shapur's household.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The ruler to whose house Rava secretly sends gifts, and whose household imprisons him.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: An earlier Sage whose saying Rava quotes: where the Sages cast their eyes comes death or poverty.

terms.meaning: From Deuteronomy 31:17: God turning away from the people, so that prayers seem to go unanswered.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara.
Cast their eyes on him: looked at him with suspicion or envy, which the text treats as bringing harm.

13.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya was at the Caesar's court when a heretic made a gesture at him meaning: your nation is the one whose Master has turned His face away from it. Rabbi Yehoshua gestured back: His hand is stretched out over us. The Caesar asked what the two had signed, and Rabbi Yehoshua explained both. Then the court asked the heretic what he had gestured and what he got in reply, and he admitted he did not know what Rabbi Yehoshua's gesture meant. They said a man who does not understand what is signed to him has no business signing before the king, and they took him out and killed him.
13.why: Rav Yosef has just said that even when God hides His face, His hand is stretched out over Israel. This story shows Rabbi Yehoshua giving that same answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage at the Caesar's court who answers a heretic's insult with a gesture of his own.

people.name: the Caesar
people.about: The Roman emperor, who asks Rabbi Yehoshua to explain the exchange.

terms.meaning: The Talmud's word for someone, often of Jewish origin, who rejects the Sages' teachings and argues against them.

14.note: Rav Kahana hid under the bed of his teacher Rav and heard him chatting and laughing with his wife and then having relations with her. Rav Kahana said aloud that Rav's mouth was like that of a man who had never tasted a cooked dish. Rav said to him: Kahana, get out, this is not proper conduct.
14.why: Rav had taught that even light talk between a man and his wife before relations is recounted to him at his death. The Gemara challenges this with Rav's own behavior, then answers that such talk is fine when he needs to win his wife's goodwill.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's student, who hides under his teacher's bed.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rav Kahana's teacher, whose private talk with his wife his student overhears.

terms.meaning: A polite phrase in the text for having marital relations.

15.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya were traveling and came to a town, where they asked whether there was a Torah scholar they could go and greet. They were told there was one, but he was blind. Rabbi Hiyya told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to stay behind so as not to lower his dignity as Nasi, and offered to go alone. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi took hold of him and went along anyway. As they left, the blind scholar blessed them: you greeted one who is seen but does not see; may you be worthy to greet the One who sees but is not seen. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said to Rabbi Hiyya that he would have kept him from this blessing.
15.why: Right after this, the visitors ask the blind scholar where his blessing comes from, and he cites Rabbi Ya'akov's teaching that whoever sees Sages in their lifetime will live, explaining why greeting a scholar earns such a reward.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; the Nasi, head of the Jewish community, who insists on visiting the blind scholar himself.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: His traveling companion, who wants to spare him the visit for the sake of his dignity.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, a position of great honor.

terms.term: the One Who sees and is not seen
terms.meaning: God, who sees everything but cannot be seen; the blessing wishes them to come before God.

16.note: Rav Idi traveled three months on the road to reach the study hall and spent only one day there before heading home, so the Sages mocked him as a student for one day. Hurt, he applied to himself the verse 'I am as one that is a laughingstock to his neighbor'. Rabbi Yohanan begged him not to bring punishment on the Sages. Then Rabbi Yohanan went to the study hall and taught that whoever studies Torah even one day a year is credited by Scripture as if he had studied all year.
16.why: The Gemara follows the blind scholar's teaching on greeting Sages with this account about honoring a scholar; it then applies Rabbi Yohanan's rule to sin as well, citing the spies' forty days that brought forty years of punishment.

people.name: Rav Idi
people.about: Father of Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi; he made a three-month journey to spend one day in the study hall.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who pleads with Rav Idi not to punish the Sages, then teaches in his defense.

terms.meaning: The study hall where Torah was taught; Rav Idi spent one day there each year.

17.note: Rav Yehuda said that a man named Hananya ben Hizkiya should be remembered for good, because without him the book of Ezekiel would have been suppressed: its words contradicted the words of the Torah. Three hundred barrels of oil were brought up to him, and he sat in an upper room and expounded the book until it was reconciled.
17.why: The Gemara has just told of a youth burned by fire for expounding the electrum in Ezekiel. A baraita after this gives another reason the Sages sought to suppress the book, the danger shown by that youth, and Hananya ben Hizkiya again defends it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports Hananya ben Hizkiya's work and praises him.

people.name: Hananya ben Hizkiya
people.about: The man who saved the book of Ezekiel by expounding it in an upper room.

terms.meaning: Withdrawn and hidden away, so that it would no longer be read as part of Scripture.
Interpreted closely, here to show that Ezekiel's laws do not truly contradict the Torah.

18.note: A youth was reading the book of Ezekiel in his teacher's house and came to understand the electrum, the mysterious radiance in Ezekiel's vision. Fire came out of the electrum and burned him. The Sages then sought to suppress the book of Ezekiel, but Hananya ben Hizkiya said to them: if this one was wise, is everyone wise?
18.why: The Gemara had asked whether the electrum may be taught at all, given a youth who was burned for it, and answered that his time had not yet come. This baraita tells that incident in full and gives Hananya ben Hizkiya's defense of the book.

people.name: Hananya ben Hizkiya
people.about: The man who argues against suppressing the book of Ezekiel after the youth's death.

terms.meaning: Hashmal: a shining substance in Ezekiel's vision of the Divine Chariot (Ezekiel 1:27). The Gemara treats understanding it as dangerous.
To withdraw a book and hide it away, so that it would no longer be read as part of Scripture.
The phrase that introduces a baraita, a teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.

19.note: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai was traveling on a donkey with his student Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh riding behind him. Rabbi Elazar asked to be taught a chapter of the Divine Chariot, and his teacher reminded him it may not be taught to one person unless he understands on his own. Rabbi Elazar asked leave to say something he had learned, and Rabban Yohanan got down from the donkey, wrapped himself, and sat on a stone under an olive tree, saying he could not ride while the Divine Presence and the angels were with them. As Rabbi Elazar expounded, fire came down from heaven and surrounded the trees, which broke into song, and an angel called from the fire that this was the very Chariot. Rabban Yohanan kissed him on the head and praised him as one who both expounds well and lives well.
19.why: The Gemara is discussing the rule that the Divine Chariot may not be taught to a single student unless he understands on his own; this baraita shows that rule at work. It is followed by a parallel scene with Rabbi Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The teacher, riding ahead on a donkey, who honors his student's teaching of the Chariot.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh
people.about: His student, who expounds the Divine Chariot before him on the road.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: Our father Abraham, whom Rabban Yohanan calls happy to have such a descendant.

terms.meaning: Maaseh Merkava: the mystical teaching drawn from Ezekiel's vision of God's throne-chariot, taught only to a select few.
The Shekhina: God's presence as felt in a particular place or moment.
The angels who serve before God.

20.note: When the story of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's teaching reached Rabbi Yehoshua, he was walking with Rabbi Yosei the Priest, and they decided to expound the Divine Chariot as well. Rabbi Yehoshua began. Although it was the summer solstice, the sky filled with clouds, something like a rainbow appeared, and the ministering angels gathered to listen, like people crowding to see a wedding. Rabbi Yosei the Priest told Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, who blessed them and their mothers and said he had dreamed of them all seated at Mount Sinai, called by a heavenly voice to great halls set out for them, their students, and their students' students, in the third group.
20.why: It follows the account of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh expounding the Chariot. The Gemara then checks both stories against a baraita listing which Sages lectured on these matters before which teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who, hearing of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's teaching, expounds the Divine Chariot himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the Priest
people.about: Rabbi Yehoshua's companion on the road, who reports what happened to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Their teacher, who blesses them and tells them his dream of Mount Sinai.

terms.meaning: Maaseh Merkava: the mystical teaching drawn from Ezekiel's vision of God's throne-chariot, taught only to a select few.
The start of the summer season, when the sky in the Land of Israel is normally clear, so clouds were a sign.
Bat kol: a voice from heaven, the way the Talmud describes God's message reaching people after prophecy ended.
In the dream, the third rank of those invited to welcome the Divine Presence.
